topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Send a request through an ordered set of possible handlers without making its caller select the final receiver. Worked example: Print-workshop request routing. Store small function handlers in a vector and use an optional destination. The vector makes order visible; the optional result separates a decline from an accepted request. One route function owns the stopping rule.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Separate routing policy from a caller.
Trace first-handler selection and explicit rejection.
Change handler order without confusing routing with validation.

blocks.text: The essential choice is handle or pass onward. The caller supplies the request and an entry point. A handler that declines allows the next handler to try. A successful handler stops this version of the chain. No handler accepting is a defined result. Order therefore affects behavior; merely calling several functions in sequence does not establish this pattern.

cards.question: What is Handler?
cards.answer: A callable that decides whether it is responsible for a request.

cards.question: What is Chain of Responsibility?
cards.answer: Ordered handlers with an explicit rule for passing or stopping requests.

cards.question: What is Optional?
cards.answer: A value wrapper that may contain one value or no value.

cards.question: What is Pipeline?
cards.answer: Stages that may each contribute work before a later stage runs.

cards.question: Why does Banana fail only in the supplied subchain demonstration?
cards.answer: The chosen entry excludes MonkeyHandler, its only accepting receiver. The remaining handlers correctly decline.

cards.question: Is a successful page check supposed to end this router?
cards.answer: No. It is a prerequisite. A destination answer ends routing; mixing those meanings would accidentally stop valid jobs before a desk is selected.

cards.question: Why does an empty optional differ from an empty string reply?
cards.answer: An empty optional means decline and continue. A present empty string is still a reply and stops the chain, so the representation separates absence from reply content.

cards.question: Why put page validation before the handler loop?
cards.answer: The input rule applies to all destinations. Without one shared gate, an early permissive rule might accept a request that later rules would reject.

cards.question: When would a map from format to handler be simpler?
cards.answer: When formats are distinct keys with no overlap or priority. A chain is useful when multiple rules can match and ordered choice is intentional.

cards.question: What regression test should accompany inserting a broad handler near the front?
cards.answer: Check requests previously handled by later specific rules. A broad match can shadow them even when its own isolated tests pass.

cards.question: Does this chain call every accepting handler?
cards.answer: No. It returns at the first present Reply. A broadcast pipeline is a different contract and needs different control flow and tests.

cards.question: Why is a vector of functions sufficient for this example?
cards.answer: Each rule has one operation and needs no exposed object state. A class hierarchy would add machinery without improving this small callable contract.

cards.question: What should happen if a Rule itself throws?
cards.answer: The supplied route does not catch it, so the exception propagates and later handlers do not run. Continuing after failure would require an explicit error policy.

topics.title: The problem: one job, one responsible desk
topics.summary: A small print workshop receives a Job containing a format name and a page count. Labels should go to a label desk; ordinary reports go to a general desk. The general desk can also print labels when the special desk is absent. Each job must reach at most one desk. The workshop rejects a page count below one or above one thousand before considering any desk. Unsupported formats must produce a visible unhandled result. No real printing happens in this teaching program: it chooses a destination so that routing can be checked without consuming supplies.

blocks.text: For two fixed destinations, an if statement is a sound start. Read the format, choose a destination, and return. There is no need to build a class family merely because several destinations exist. The limit appears when different workshop shifts need different ordered sets of rules. Copying the whole function for each shift also copies validation and fallback behavior. One shift may then accept zero-page jobs while another rejects them. We need to assemble the choices while keeping the routing contract in one place.

topics.title: Make each choice a small, honest question
topics.summary: A handler is a piece of code that accepts a request, decides whether it can handle it, and reports that decision. A chain of responsibility is an ordered set of these handlers. The delivered program represents each handler as a function. Rule is a short name, introduced by using, for std::function<Reply(const Job&)>. This standard wrapper can hold different callable objects with the same call shape. Here the shape means: borrow a read-only Job and return a Reply. The program does not need a next pointer inside every handler because a vector already stores their order.

blocks.text: Reply is std::optional<std::string>: it contains either one destination string or no string. std::nullopt explicitly means there is no answer here. That is different from an answer whose string happens to be empty. The if (reply) condition asks whether a value exists. The expression *reply then accesses that value; the asterisk is safe because the presence check came first. A missing answer is ordinary control flow, not an exception. The caller receives a separate text result, unhandled, only after every handler declines.

topics.title: Follow control and data through the chain
topics.summary: route first checks the page count. The test uses ||, meaning that either bad bound is enough to reject the job. Valid jobs enter a range-based for loop. In for (const auto& rule : rules), the colon means take each item from rules in order. auto obtains the function-wrapper type from the vector; the reference avoids copying that wrapper; const prevents this loop from changing it. The same read-only Job is borrowed by each call. No handler owns the job, stores its address, or extends its lifetime.

blocks.text: For a label job, label_rule returns a value, so route returns immediately. general_rule is never called for that request. For a report, the first handler returns no value and the second supplies the destination. For archive, both decline. The compiler checks that each stored callable has the required input and result shape. Which handler supplies the answer is decided during execution from the job and the order of rules. Moving the rules into a different vector can change behavior without recompiling route, although changing the source initializer still requires rebuilding the executable.

topics.title: First-handler routing is not an all-stage pipeline
topics.summary: A pipeline is a sequence in which several stages may each perform part of the work. A document pipeline might validate pages, add a tracking code, write a record, and print. Success at one stage normally means continue. Our chain has a different rule: an answer means stop. If a maintainer converts return *reply into an assignment and continues looping, the general desk can replace the label desk because both accept labels. With real printing, that same mistake could produce two copies. The word chain alone does not tell a reader which stopping rule applies.

blocks.text: Decide the rule before choosing an interface. In a validation pipeline, an enum such as Continue or Reject makes sense; in this router, optional destination makes sense. Mixing both meanings in one bool makes it hard to tell whether true means finished or allowed to continue. Shared requirements such as a valid page count belong before routing. A handler that is optional in one configuration must not be the only place that enforces a mandatory check. The empty-rule test proves that having no handlers remains a defined situation.

topics.title: Boundaries, costs, and a practical review
topics.summary: The handlers are pure selection functions: their result depends on the job, and they do not print, store files, or change outside data. This makes order tests cheap and repeatable. With n handlers, an unsupported request makes n calls; an early match needs fewer. std::function offers runtime flexibility but may allocate when storing a large callable. For this tiny fixed router, direct calls or a table of plain function pointers can cost less. Neither performance claim should replace a measurement if routing is on a busy path.

blocks.text: Before adding a rule in real software, inspect overlap, position, failure meaning, and ownership. A fallback placed first can hide every special case. A rule that captures a local reference and survives that local variable can later access a dead object. The current vector stores free functions, so it has no such captured lifetime. A linked chain would also need a no-cycle rule; this vector traversal has no link cycle to create. The model deliberately omits retries and external actions. Choosing a destination successfully does not prove that the destination later completed the job.

topics.title: Exercise 13.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: Explain in three sentences why an accepted destination must not also mean the printer completed the job.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Separate routing from an outside effect.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: Routing identifies responsibility. A printer may later be offline or run out of paper. Keep a separate delivery result and retry policy so routing success does not hide an external failure.

workshop.title: Print-workshop request routing
workshop.problem: Print-workshop request routing. Reject page counts outside 1 through 1000 before routing. Choose the first willing handler; expose unsupported formats. Allow the same handlers to be arranged in another order.
workshop.output:
label desk
general desk
unhandled

steps.why: Two pages lies inside the common valid range.
The optional contains a string; route returns it.
general_rule now gets a chance and answers general desk.
The count check ends route before any rule is called.

workshop.pitfall: Continue through the vector after finding a destination. A label job can finish as general desk instead of label desk. The two handlers overlap, so the last answer replaces the first.

discussion.question: Choose between this chain and a switch for three permanently fixed format codes with no overlap.
discussion.answer: A switch is reasonable because a fixed direct mapping needs no configurable search. Choose the chain if fallback order or independently added rules is a real requirement, and test overlap explicitly.

workshop.alternative: A direct if/else chain is clearer when the choices and their order never vary. Virtual Handler classes suit handlers with substantial private state, but would add unnecessary lifetime machinery to these two stateless rules.
workshop.design: Store small function handlers in a vector and use an optional destination. The vector makes order visible; the optional result separates a decline from an accepted request. One route function owns the stopping rule.
invariants: A valid job receives at most one destination.
Every handler sees the same unchanged job.
Rejected counts never enter a handler.
workshop.maintenance: A new destination becomes one independently testable rule. Configuration reviews must still examine overlaps and order because individual handler tests cannot establish the whole routing policy.
workshop.verification: The program checks label/report/unknown cases, both invalid count sides, the largest valid count, an empty chain, and reversed order. It verifies selection behavior, not print hardware or concurrent changes to rules.
